source.title: Despite "super-human" performance, current LLMs are unsuited for decisions about ethics and safety
source.authors: Joshua Albrecht; Ellie Kitanidis; Abraham J. Fetterman

record.tranche_reason: The study reports downstream ETHICS-C-S performance at different GPT-3 sizes and says some examples show inverse scaling. It does not test held-out cross-entropy power laws or compute-optimal allocations.
record.gate_note: Only the downstream-performance-with-scale aspect of V6 is tested. The paper reports aggregate ETHICS-C-S accuracy for named GPT-3 size/version settings and a qualitative inverse-scaling result for some examples. The SimPrompting result, human scores, random-label prompt result, rewording attacks, and chain-of-thought results are not rows because they do not measure downstream performance as a function of scale.
record.test_reason: Section 6.1 tracks GPT-3 confidence on misclassified ETHICS-C-S examples across 4 model sizes. It reports inverse scaling on some examples and argues scale is unlikely to fix these errors. This bears on V6 (downstream improvement with scale), but only on a subset of examples selected for being misclassified.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly right, but slightly overstated. The authors say scale is 'unlikely to completely solve these issues' and 'could even make some issues worse'. They also say scaling and chain-of-thought are currently insufficient to address the failures.
record.recipe_differences: The study measures prompted ethical-classification accuracy and example-level confidence across GPT-3 sizes, rather than held-out cross-entropy loss across parameter, token, or compute sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported aggregate accuracy varies across the named GPT-3 size/version settings; the paper also reports inverse scaling for some individual examples.
record.peer_reviewed: ML Safety Workshop, 36th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2022)
record.problems: The study uses ETHICS-C-S rather than held-out pretraining loss; it gives no parameter counts, token or compute sweeps, fitted laws, or extrapolation tests. The inverse-scaling figure's numeric values and individual model-size labels are not available in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows for SimPrompter, humans, random-label prompting, rewording, or chain-of-thought are included: those results do not measure downstream performance as a function of scale. See Table 1 and Sections 5–6 and Appendix F.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining loss vs parameters, tokens or compute; no power-law fits.
Depth, width or other shape effects at fixed parameter count.
Whole-test-set downstream accuracy vs scale from the study's own runs, any fitted predictive relation, the link to pretraining loss, and tasks beyond ETHICS-C-S.
Dependence of exponents or compute-optimal split on setup and fitting choices.

missing.what: Per-size confidence distributions and parameter counts for the 4 GPT-3 sizes on misclassified examples; whole-test-set accuracy at each size is not reported

record.verdict_notes: The record's 'supports' label rested on r1 and r2, which appear to be cited ETHICS-paper numbers rather than the study's own runs. That label is removed. The study's only own scaling evidence is the inverse-scaling figure on selected misclassified examples.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute; power-law fits and several-orders-of-magnitude ranges.
Whether power laws fitted on small runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocations and their trends with compute.
Effects of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
The study evaluates one ethical-classification dataset and does not test pretraining-loss correlations, a fitted predictive relationship, or downstream tasks beyond ETHICS-C-S.
Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocations on setup and fitting choices, and bending of fitted loss curves.

rows.subject: GPT-3 (smallest model, 2019)
rows.size_stated: smallest model; parameter count not stated
rows.operation_detail: Evaluate ETHICS-C-S test-set classification accuracy at a GPT-3 model size.
rows.note: The table gives an aggregate score; it does not provide a fitted scaling relationship.
rows.check: Cited result, not the study's own run. The 2019 smallest-model score has no uncertainty and comes from the original ETHICS paper setup (Hendrycks et al.). It should not support a verdict here.

rows.subject: GPT-3 (largest model, 2019)
rows.size_stated: largest model; parameter count not stated
rows.operation_detail: Evaluate ETHICS-C-S test-set classification accuracy at a GPT-3 model size.
rows.note: Compared with the smallest 2019 GPT-3 model in Table 1, the largest model has higher aggregate accuracy.
rows.check: Cited result. Appendix I calls this 'the GPT-3 model used in the original ETHICS paper'. It is not the study's own scaling measurement.

rows.subject: GPT-3 (largest model, current)
rows.size_stated: largest model; parameter count not stated
rows.uncertainty: ± 0.1; Table 1 reports confidence interval (1 std across 3 seeds)
rows.note: This is a largest-model version score; the text does not give a corresponding current-version score for smaller model sizes.
rows.check: A single largest-model score (92.5%) with no comparison across sizes, so it cannot show a scaling effect. Its 'current' model version also differs from the 2019 rows, which mixes in a model-version change.

rows.subject: GPT-3 (four model sizes; individual size names not stated)
rows.size_stated: four model sizes; parameter counts not stated in the text
rows.operation_detail: Compare confidence in predictions on misclassified ETHICS-C-S examples across four model sizes.
rows.measure: direction of change in confidence in the wrong answer with model scale
rows.note: The text explicitly says some scenarios show inverse scaling, with the model becoming increasingly certain of the wrong answer as size increases. The individual figure values and size labels are not present in the text.
rows.check: Reversed only for some examples, and those examples were selected because the model misclassified them. Error-conditioned selection can produce apparent inverse scaling. The values are figure-only. Accuracy across the 4 sizes over the whole test set is not reported.

relationships.condition: GPT-3, 4 sizes, a subset of ETHICS-C-S test examples selected for being misclassified
relationships.reason: Confidence in the wrong answer rises with model size on some selected examples, so downstream improvement is not uniform per example (r4). It is figure-only, and selecting on errors weakens the evidence.
relationships.display_finding: Confidence in incorrect answers increases with size on some examples selected for misclassification, although selecting errors weakens the evidence.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Aggregate ETHICS-C-S accuracy for the reported 2019 GPT-3 size endpoints and the current largest model
reader_labels.reason: The reported aggregate accuracy is higher for the largest 2019 model than for the smallest, and the current largest model also has high accuracy (r1, r2, r3); the study does not establish a predictive scaling curve.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Some individual misclassified ETHICS-C-S scenarios across model sizes
reader_labels.reason: For some examples, confidence in the wrong answer increases with scale, contrary to uniformly improving downstream behavior (r4).
